content: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria Definitions: In women, asymptomatic bacteriuria is defined as the presence of the same bacterial strain in two consecutive voided urine specimens, each with a quantitative count of ≥ 10⁵ colony-forming units (CFU) per milliliter. In men, it is defined as a single, clean-catch voided urine specimen with one bacterial species isolated in a quantitative count of ≥ 10⁵ CFU/mL. For catheterized urine specimens, it is defined as a single catheterized urine specimen with one bacterial species isolated in a quantitative count of ≥ 10² CFU/mL. Causative Pathogens: Common pathogens include Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, coagulase-negative staphylococci, Enterococcus, Group B streptococci, Gardnerella vaginalis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus mirabilis, Providencia stuartii, and Morganella morganii. The latter group is more common in patients with long-term urologic devices. Empiric Antimicrobial Therapy: Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria is not recommended for the following groups: Premenopausal, nonpregnant women Diabetic women Older adults residing in the community Elderly individuals in long-term care facilities Patients with spinal cord injuries Patients with indwelling urethral catheters while the catheter remains in place Specific Considerations: Men: Screening or treatment for asymptomatic bacteriuria is not recommended. Premenopausal, nonpregnant women: Screening or treatment is not indicated. Pregnant women: Treatment is recommended, with preferred regimens including: 1. Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally twice daily for 3–5 days (avoid in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency). 2. Amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 3–5 days. 3. Amoxicillin-clavulanate 500 mg orally twice daily for 3–5 days. 4. Cephalexin 500 mg orally three times daily for 3–5 days. 5. Fosfomycin 3 g as a single dose. 6. Trimethoprim orally twice daily for 3–5 days (only after the first trimester). Diabetic women: Screening or treatment is not recommended. Older adults in the community: Screening or treatment is not recommended. Elderly institutionalized individuals: Screening or treatment is not recommended. Patients with spinal cord injuries: Screening or treatment is not recommended. Patients with indwelling urethral catheters: Screening or treatment is not recommended while the catheter remains in place. Urologic interventions: Screening or treatment is recommended before transurethral resection of the prostate. Scabies Preferred Regimen: Permethrin cream (5%) applied to all areas of the body from the neck down and washed off after 8–14 hours. Alternatively, ivermectin 200 µg/kg orally, repeated in 2 weeks. Alternative Regimens: Lindane (1%) solution or gel. Imiquimod 5% cream. Sinecatechins 15% ointment. Provider-Administered Treatments: Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen or cryoprobe, repeated every 1–2 weeks. Podophyllin resin 10–25% in compound tincture of benzoin. Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) or bichloroacetic acid (BCA) 80–90%. Surgical removal via tangential scissor excision, shave excision, curettage, or electrosurgery. Trichomoniasis (Trichomonas vaginalis) Preferred Regimen: Metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose. Tinidazole 2 g orally in a single dose. Alternative Regimen: Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. Pregnancy Considerations: Metronidazole 2 g orally in a single dose can be administered at any stage of pregnancy. Breastfeeding should be withheld during treatment and for 12–24 hours after the last dose to minimize infant exposure. Genital Herpes First Episode: Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 7–10 days. Alternatively, valacyclovir 1 g orally twice daily for 7–10 days. Recurrent Episodes: Suppressive therapy: Acyclovir 400 mg orally twice daily or valacyclovir 500–1000 mg orally once daily. Episodic therapy: Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times daily for 5 days or valacyclovir 500 mg orally twice daily for 3 days. Severe Genital Herpes: Acyclovir 5–10 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours for 2–7 days, followed by oral antiviral therapy to complete at least 10 days of total treatment. HIV-Infected Patients: Suppressive therapy: Acyclovir 400–800 mg orally twice to three times daily or valacyclovir 500 mg orally twice daily. Acyclovir-Resistant Herpes: Foscarnet 40 mg/kg intravenously every 8 hours until clinical resolution. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) Parenteral Treatment: Preferred regimen: Cefotetan 2 g IV every 12 hours or cefoxitin 2 g IV every 6 hours, combined with doxycycline 100 mg orally or IV every 12 hours. Alternative regimen: Ampicillin/sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours, combined with doxycycline 100 mg orally or IV every 12 hours. Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis Preferred Regimens: Nitrofurantoin monohydrate/macrocrystals 100 mg twice daily for 5 days. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg (one double-strength tablet) twice daily for 3 days. Fosfomycin trometamol 3 g as a single dose. Alternative Regimens: Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) for 3 days. β-lactam agents (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefdinir) for 3–7 days.
